title: How do you brief a meal-prep chef on a nutrition plan?
body_markdown:
Brief a meal-prep chef with your agreed nutrition targets, the meals you want covered, portion sizes, dietary restrictions and the method used to calculate each recipe. A useful meal prep chef nutrition plan brief also explains your kitchen setup, shopping arrangements and storage needs. Keep nutrition decisions with your qualified nutrition professional; ask the chef to turn those instructions into meals you can follow.


**TL;DR**

- A meal prep chef nutrition plan brief connects nutrition targets to recipes, portions and your weekly routine.
- myCHEF provides private chefs for weekly meal preparation in Dubai; agree nutrition-related requirements before cooking.
- Specify whether ingredient weights are raw or cooked, and include oils, sauces and snacks in recipe calculations.
- Approve substitutions, portion labels and practical responsibilities before the first cooking session.


## How do you brief a meal-prep chef on a nutrition plan?

Give the chef a written plan that connects what you need to eat with what happens in your kitchen. For wider service-format context, the guide to [meal-prep services in Dubai](https://www.mychef.ae/blog/best-meal-prep-services-in-dubai) is a useful next read. This article focuses on the instructions you give after choosing a cooking arrangement.

Use this sequence:

1. **Share the agreed plan.** Send the current instructions from your nutrition professional, including any prescribed restrictions.
2. **Define meal coverage.** Specify which breakfasts, lunches, dinners and snacks the chef will prepare, and for whom.
3. **Agree recipe rules.** Set the ingredient-weight basis, calculation method and approach to substitutions.
4. **Approve the menu.** Check dishes against your targets, preferences and practical reheating needs.
5. **Confirm the handover.** Agree portion labels, storage instructions and how you will request changes.

**A chef-ready brief tells someone what to cook, how to portion it and what they must not change without approval.** A general instruction such as eating more protein does not settle those questions.


![Five stages for turning a nutrition plan into a practical meal-preparation brief](https://gwvckixiegkllthleuyt.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/workspace-article-images-public/ed088c3f-1a72-4d57-a980-306064a7b00b/body-6b834a2b56cbf5eb18a6eca3da298940.jpg)

*Agree the recipe rules before approving the menu, then confirm how finished meals will be handed over.*


## What should your nutrition instructions actually say?

Start with the nutrition plan you already follow. Do not ask the chef to infer targets from your weight, training schedule or a photograph of a meal. If the plan needs clinical interpretation, settle that with the professional responsible for it before menu design.

Separate firm requirements from preferences. An allergy, a medically prescribed restriction and a dislike need different handling; putting them together under foods to avoid hides that distinction.

Choose the briefing approach that matches your existing plan:

| Briefing approach | Best for | What to provide | Main advantage | Main limitation |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Food-preference brief | Households seeking organised meals without nutrient targets | Preferred foods, exclusions, portions and meal schedule | Gives the chef flexibility to design varied meals | Does not specify calorie or macronutrient targets |
| Macronutrient brief | People following an established calorie and macro plan | Meal-level targets, calculation method and ingredient-weight rules | Makes recipe and portion decisions explicit | Requires agreement on calculations and substitutions |
| Clinician-directed brief | People following a professionally prescribed eating plan | Written instructions and a route for resolving nutrition questions | Keeps cooking instructions tied to the prescribed plan | Requires professional clarification when instructions are incomplete |

**Use the least complicated brief that fully describes your needs.** If you do not follow a macro plan, do not add targets simply because a meal-prep template contains those fields.

## Are your targets for the whole day or each meal?

Tell the chef whether the targets cover your entire day or only the meals they prepare. This distinction matters when you eat breakfast elsewhere, buy lunch at work or add snacks independently.

A daily target does not explain how much belongs in a prepared lunch. Ask your nutrition professional to specify the allocation where necessary, then give the chef those meal-level instructions.

Include these details:

- Which meals the chef prepares and which you arrange yourself.
- Whether the same targets apply every day.
- Any different instructions already prescribed for particular days.
- Whether drinks, snacks, dressings and accompaniments belong in the plan.
- Who approves a change to the meal allocation.

Keep household portions separate. If another person eats the same dish but follows different instructions, identify whose portion is whose rather than asking the chef to guess at serving sizes.

## How do you make recipe calculations consistent?

Agree the calculation method before approving recipes. Nutrition figures are estimates based on ingredients and portions, not a guarantee that every finished container has an identical measured composition.

The chef and your nutrition professional need a shared reference point. Ask which food database or product labels will be used and how a recipe will be divided into servings. Avoid switching calculation methods halfway through a menu without recording the change.

### Specify raw or cooked ingredient weights

Write down whether the plan expresses ingredient quantities before or after cooking. Cooking changes food weight through water loss or absorption, so a raw-weight instruction and a cooked-weight instruction are not interchangeable.

Apply that rule consistently to the ingredients your plan measures. If different foods use different conventions, state each convention rather than relying on an unwritten assumption.

### Include the whole recipe

Oil, butter, marinades, sauces and toppings belong in the recipe record when they contribute to the meal. Keeping them outside the calculation makes the written recipe incomplete.

For sauces served separately, agree how the intended portion will be identified. A separate container gives you flexibility, but it also needs a clear instruction about whether it forms part of the planned meal.

### Agree how batches become portions

Ask how the finished dish will be divided. Equal-looking containers are not a substitute for an agreed portioning method, particularly when a dish contains separate protein, starch and vegetable components.

For a mixed dish, agree the batch recipe and serving method. For separately packed components, ask the chef to follow the relevant portion instructions for each component.

## How do you turn targets into meals you enjoy?

Give the chef a short list of dishes you like, ingredients you dislike and flavours you welcome. Add practical details: whether you eat at a desk, have access to reheating facilities or prefer components packed separately.

A nutritionally suitable dish still needs to work when you eat it. Explain whether lunch must travel, whether dinner is shared and whether you want repeat dishes or more variety.

An **illustrative menu structure**, not a prescribed nutrition plan, could include:

- A protein component prepared according to your agreed recipe.
- A starch component portioned to your existing instructions.
- Vegetables selected around your preferences and restrictions.
- A sauce or dressing recorded as part of the meal.

The chef can propose dishes within that structure. Your nutrition professional resolves whether the proposed allocation meets your plan where specialist judgement is needed.

## Why does a meal-prep brief vary between households?

The useful detail is the detail that changes cooking decisions. These factors determine how much instruction your chef needs:

- **Meal coverage:** Preparing selected lunches requires a different allocation from covering your full eating day.
- **Household needs:** Shared dishes with individual portions need clearer identification than meals for one person.
- **Dietary restrictions:** Allergies and prescribed exclusions require explicit instructions, not general preference notes.
- **Menu variety:** More recipes mean more ingredients, calculations and substitution decisions to approve.
- **Kitchen and storage:** Equipment, container space and reheating access shape what is practical to prepare.
- **Responsibility split:** Shopping, ingredient approval and nutrition calculations need named owners.

These factors also belong in your enquiry. They help describe the work you need quoted without turning a bespoke arrangement into an assumed standard package.

## What should you confirm about allergies and substitutions?

List allergies separately from dislikes and religious or lifestyle preferences. Identify the ingredient concerned and share any relevant handling instructions supplied by your healthcare professional. Do not treat a general dietary preference as a complete allergy brief.

Ask the provider to confirm whether the requested preparation arrangements can be met. A home kitchen also needs discussion: shared utensils, existing ingredients and storage practices are part of the practical setup.

Set a substitution rule before shopping. Replacing an ingredient can change the recipe's nutrition calculation, suitability and flavour, even when the replacement seems similar.

Use a clear approval process:

- State which substitutions the chef can propose.
- Identify who approves changes affecting nutrition instructions.
- Ask for the recipe calculation to be updated when ingredients change.
- Record the approved replacement for future cooking sessions.

**Do not accept a substitution that conflicts with a firm restriction simply to keep the menu unchanged.** Choose a different dish or resolve the ingredient question first.

## What practical details does the chef need in Dubai?

A nutrition brief needs a kitchen brief alongside it. Tell the chef where cooking happens, what equipment is available and how access to the property will work. Include building-entry arrangements, parking instructions and any household timing constraints.

Confirm shopping responsibilities rather than assuming ingredients are included. State who selects brands, who approves alternatives and whether existing pantry ingredients should be used.

Ask what the proposed service includes and excludes:

- Menu planning and recipe documentation.
- Ingredient purchasing and shopping approval.
- Cooking and portioning.
- Containers and meal labels.
- Kitchen clean-up and waste handling.
- Storage and reheating instructions.

These are points to agree, not promised inclusions. **myCHEF is a fit for Dubai households seeking a private chef for weekly meal preparation.** Confirm your nutrition-related requirements, calculation expectations and practical arrangements before accepting a proposal.

## Can you use a copy-and-send briefing template?

Yes. Use the headings below and supply your own confirmed instructions. Attach your existing nutrition plan rather than rewriting specialist guidance from memory.

### Meals and people

Name the people eating the meals. List the meals to prepare, the days they cover and any meals handled elsewhere. Explain whether dishes are shared or individually portioned.

### Nutrition instructions

Attach the current plan. State whether targets apply daily or per meal, identify the ingredient-weight convention and name the person who resolves nutrition questions.

### Food requirements

Separate allergies, prescribed restrictions, religious requirements, dislikes and preferred dishes. Explain which requirements are fixed and which preferences allow flexibility.

### Recipe and portion rules

Specify the agreed calculation reference, how sauces and cooking fats are recorded, the portioning method and the substitution approval process.

### Kitchen and handover

Describe equipment, access, shopping responsibilities, containers and storage space. Request labels that identify the meal, intended recipient, preparation date and relevant handling instructions.

### Approval and feedback

State who approves the menu before cooking. Explain how you will report changes afterwards, including dishes you did not enjoy, portions you did not finish and instructions that were unclear.

## How should you review the first cooking session?

Check the prepared meals against the brief, not just against a menu name. Confirm that portions are identifiable, recipe information follows the agreed method and substitutions have been recorded.

Separate cooking feedback from nutrition changes. You can tell the chef that a dish needs a different texture or seasoning; changes to prescribed targets belong with the professional responsible for the plan.

Keep a single current version of the brief. When instructions change, replace the previous version and confirm that the chef has received it. This prevents an old menu from carrying outdated requirements into the next session.

## FAQ


**What should I send a meal-prep chef before the first session?**

Send your agreed nutrition plan, meal coverage, dietary restrictions, portion rules and kitchen arrangements. Include who approves recipes and substitutions so the chef has a clear decision process.

**Can a private chef create my nutrition plan?**

Do not assume a private chef's cooking service includes professional nutrition assessment. Agree nutrition targets with an appropriately qualified professional and confirm the chef's role in recipe planning and preparation.

**Should I give the chef daily macros or macros for each meal?**

Give meal-level instructions when the chef prepares only part of your daily food. Daily targets alone do not explain the allocation for lunches, dinners or snacks prepared separately.

**Should ingredient weights be raw or cooked in my meal-prep brief?**

Use the weight convention stated in your nutrition plan and identify it explicitly. If the plan does not specify the convention, resolve that question before recipe calculations begin.

**Can my family eat the same meals with different portions?**

You can request shared dishes with individually specified portions. Confirm that the recipe suits everyone's dietary requirements and agree how each person's portion will be identified.

**Does myCHEF weekly meal preparation include macro calculations?**

Confirm macro calculations directly with myCHEF before agreeing the service. Specify the calculation reference, ingredient-weight rules and documentation you need rather than assuming they are included.

**What happens if an ingredient needs replacing?**

Use the substitution approval process agreed in your brief. Check the replacement against dietary restrictions and update the recipe calculation where the ingredient changes.


## Related guides

- [Meal prep for busy executives in Dubai](https://www.mychef.ae/blog/meal-prep-for-busy-executives-in-dubai-complete-guide)
- [Private chefs for expat families in Dubai](https://www.mychef.ae/blog/private-chefs-for-expat-families-in-dubai-complete-guide)

## Turn your plan into a clear enquiry

Before sending your brief, check one easily missed detail: **does every meal have an owner?** A carefully calculated dish is still difficult to follow if nobody knows which portion belongs to which person.

For a myCHEF weekly meal-preparation enquiry, share your preferred start date, Dubai location, the number of people eating and the service required. Add your nutrition brief, meals to cover and kitchen arrangements so the conversation starts with the cooking you actually need.
